title: Vitamins for Hangover: B-Complex, Thiamine, and Vitamin C Explained
excerpt: Do vitamins help a hangover? What alcohol actually depletes, what B-complex, thiamine (B1), and vitamin C can and can't fix, safe upper limits, and when heavy drinkers need a doctor.
metaDescription: Do vitamins help a hangover? What alcohol really depletes, what B-complex, thiamine, and vitamin C can and can't fix, and safe upper limits to know.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** vitamins are not a hangover cure. One night of drinking does not leave a well-fed adult deficient in B vitamins or vitamin C, and no good human trial shows that a vitamin pill makes a hangover go away. What alcohol does do is increase how much of some nutrients you lose in urine, and, over months of heavy drinking, it seriously drains thiamine (vitamin B1), folate, and a few others. So vitamins matter a lot for regular heavy drinkers and very little for the occasional big night. This guide walks through what alcohol actually depletes, what taking B-complex, B1, or vitamin C can and can't fix, how much is sensible, and when a "hangover" is really a sign you need a doctor.

**The quick rules:** If you drink occasionally, a basic B-complex or multivitamin with breakfast is cheap and low-risk, but don't expect it to change how you feel the next morning. Water, food, sleep, and drinking less do far more. If you drink heavily most days, the vitamin you should care about is thiamine, and the right move is to talk to a doctor, not to self-treat with a hangover product. Stay under the safe upper limits for vitamin B6, niacin, and vitamin C, which are easy to exceed if you stack several "hangover" products.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **See a doctor if** you drink heavily most days, you have numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, you notice confusion, unsteady walking, or unusual eye movements, you have liver or kidney disease, you are pregnant, or you take prescription medication. Confusion, poor balance, and abnormal eye movements in someone who drinks heavily can be signs of Wernicke's encephalopathy, a thiamine emergency. In that situation, get emergency care (call 911 in the US). Do not wait to see if a supplement helps.

## What a Hangover Actually Is (and Why That Matters for Vitamins)

Before looking at any single vitamin, it helps to know what a vitamin would have to fix. Researchers still don't have a complete explanation of hangovers, but the main contributors are reasonably well understood:

- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before breaking it down further into acetate. Acetaldehyde is linked to nausea, flushing, and the general poisoned feeling.
- **Inflammation and immune signaling.** Studies have found raised levels of inflammatory messengers (cytokines) the morning after heavy drinking, and hangover severity tracks with them in some research.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep, so you wake up unrested.
- **Fluid loss.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate more than you drink.
- **Low blood sugar and stomach irritation.** Alcohol can lower blood sugar in some people and irritates the stomach lining.
- **Congeners.** Darker drinks carry more by-products of fermentation, which seem to make hangovers worse for some people. We cover this more in our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

Notice what's missing from that list: "vitamin deficiency." A hangover is not mainly a nutrient problem. That single point explains why vitamins disappoint people who expect them to work like a painkiller. They can support some of the machinery involved in clearing alcohol and repairing damage, but they don't target the main drivers of how you feel at 9 a.m.

For the full picture of what drives a hangover and what helps, see our [complete guide to curing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide).

## What Alcohol Actually Depletes: An Honest Breakdown

Here is where the internet tends to exaggerate. You'll read that alcohol "flushes out" all your vitamins. The truth depends heavily on how much and how often you drink.

### After one night of drinking

For a healthy person who eats normally, one night of drinking does a few things to nutrients:

- **More water-soluble nutrients leave in urine.** Because you're urinating more, you lose more of what's dissolved in it. That includes some B vitamins and vitamin C, plus minerals such as magnesium, zinc, and potassium. Alcohol has a well-documented effect on increasing magnesium and zinc losses through the kidneys.
- **Absorption may be dulled for a while.** Alcohol irritates the gut lining and can reduce how well certain nutrients, thiamine in particular, are absorbed while it's present.
- **You probably ate badly.** Skipped dinner, late-night fast food, or vomiting all reduce what you take in.

What this does **not** add up to is a deficiency. Your body holds stores of most vitamins that last days to months (vitamin B12 stores can last years). A single night can nudge levels down a little, but it does not produce the kind of shortage that causes symptoms. If you feel terrible the next morning, it isn't because you've run out of B vitamins.

### After months or years of heavy drinking

This is where vitamins become a real medical issue. Regular heavy drinking is one of the most common causes of vitamin deficiency in wealthy countries, for several reasons working together:

- **Alcohol replaces food.** Alcohol carries calories but no vitamins, and heavy drinkers often eat less.
- **Absorption drops.** Alcohol damages the gut lining and interferes with how the intestine takes up thiamine and folate.
- **The liver stores less.** A damaged liver holds and activates vitamins less effectively.
- **Losses go up.** Urinary losses of some nutrients rise with chronic use.

The nutrients most commonly low in people with alcohol use disorder are:

| Nutrient | Why alcohol affects it | What a real deficiency can cause |
|---|---|---|
| Thiamine (B1) | Reduced absorption, reduced storage and activation, poor intake | Wernicke's encephalopathy, Korsakoff syndrome, nerve damage, heart problems |
| Folate (B9) | Poor intake, reduced absorption, increased urinary loss | A type of anemia with large red blood cells |
| Vitamin B6 | Alcohol's by-products speed up its breakdown | Nerve problems, skin and mouth changes |
| Vitamin B12 | Less common, but gut and liver damage can contribute | Anemia, nerve damage |
| Niacin (B3) | Poor intake, heavy demand from alcohol metabolism | Pellagra (rare today, but still seen in severe alcohol use) |
| Vitamin C | Poor diet, possibly increased use | Fatigue, gum problems, poor wound healing; scurvy in severe cases |
| Magnesium, zinc | Increased urinary losses, poor intake | Muscle cramps, weakness, poor immune function |

Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) can also fall in people with liver disease, but those are clinical problems handled by a doctor, not hangover issues.

The key takeaway: the depletion story is real, but it belongs mostly to **regular heavy drinking**, not to the occasional big night out.

## Thiamine (Vitamin B1): The One That Actually Matters

If you only remember one vitamin from this page, make it thiamine.

### Why alcohol and thiamine are such a bad pair

Thiamine is needed to turn food (especially carbohydrates) into usable energy, and the brain and nerves depend on it heavily. Your body stores only a small amount, enough for a matter of weeks. Alcohol attacks thiamine from every direction: it reduces absorption in the gut, reduces how much the liver can store, and reduces the conversion of thiamine into its active form. Heavy drinkers also tend to eat less of it.

When thiamine runs low for long enough, the result can be **Wernicke's encephalopathy**, a medical emergency. The classic signs are confusion, unsteady walking, and abnormal eye movements, although many patients don't show all three. Left untreated, it can progress to **Korsakoff syndrome**, a long-lasting memory disorder. This is why hospitals routinely give thiamine (often by injection or IV) to people admitted with heavy alcohol use, and why clinical guidelines in the UK and elsewhere recommend thiamine for people being treated for alcohol dependence or withdrawal.

### Does thiamine help a normal hangover?

There's no good evidence that it does. Thiamine isn't involved in the main causes of a hangover in a well-nourished person, and there are no solid trials showing that taking B1 before or after drinking makes the next morning better.

That doesn't make thiamine pointless for drinkers. For someone who drinks heavily and regularly, keeping thiamine topped up is a sensible protective step, and oral thiamine is inexpensive and very low risk. There's no established upper limit for oral thiamine because excess is cleared in urine. But a pill on the nightstand is not a substitute for medical care if signs of real deficiency appear, and people with severe deficiency often need injected thiamine because oral absorption is too poor.

**Bottom line on B1:** low value for the occasional drinker's hangover, real value as a safety measure for people who drink heavily. If that second group includes you, the conversation to have is with a doctor, who may also want to talk about your drinking itself.

## B-Complex for Hangovers: What It Can and Can't Do

B-complex products combine several B vitamins (usually B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B9, and B12). They're the most common vitamin in "hangover" formulas. Here's what the evidence supports for each claim you'll see.

### "B vitamins help your body process alcohol"

Partly true, but it doesn't mean what marketers imply. The enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde rely on a helper molecule called NAD, which your body builds from niacin (B3). In theory, that links niacin to alcohol metabolism. In practice, a well-fed person has plenty of niacin, and there's no good evidence that taking extra speeds up how fast you clear alcohol or acetaldehyde. Your liver processes alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, and vitamins don't change that rate in any meaningful way.

### "B vitamins reduce hangover symptoms"

The evidence here is thin. A few points worth knowing:

- **An observational study.** Researchers in the Netherlands (Verster and colleagues, *Journal of Clinical Medicine*, 2019) compared people's normal diets with their reported hangover severity and found that people who ate more nicotinic acid (a form of niacin, B3) and zinc reported somewhat less severe hangovers. This is interesting, but it's an observational link from food intake, not a test of taking a pill before drinking. It doesn't prove cause and effect.
- **An old pyritinol trial.** A small trial from the 1970s tested pyritinol, a synthetic compound related to vitamin B6, and reported fewer hangover symptoms. It was small and has not been convincingly repeated, and pyritinol is not the same as the B6 in a normal supplement.
- **Systematic reviews.** A widely cited review in the *BMJ* (Pittler, Verster, and Ernst, 2005) looked at trials of hangover remedies and concluded there was no compelling evidence that any conventional or complementary treatment effectively prevents or treats hangover. Later reviews have reached similar conclusions: some remedies show small or early promise, but the trials are few and small.

So B-complex sits in the "plausible, cheap, unproven for hangovers" category.

### "B vitamins give you energy"

Only if you were low. B vitamins help your body use energy from food, but taking more when you already have enough doesn't create extra energy. The bright yellow urine you get after a B-complex is mostly riboflavin (B2) leaving your body, not a sign it's working.

### When B-complex does make sense

- **You drink regularly and your diet is patchy.** A daily B-complex or multivitamin is a reasonable insurance policy. It's not a license to drink more.
- **You're following a restrictive diet.** Vegans, for example, need a reliable B12 source regardless of drinking.
- **A doctor has found you're low.** Then you treat the deficiency, at the dose they recommend.

For a wider look at which ingredients in hangover products have evidence behind them, see our [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025).

## Vitamin C for Hangovers

Vitamin C gets its own section because so many people reach for an orange juice or an effervescent tablet the morning after.

### The case for it

Vitamin C is an antioxidant, and alcohol metabolism produces oxidative stress (a build-up of reactive molecules that can damage cells). In animal studies, vitamin C has reduced some markers of alcohol-related liver stress, and some lab research suggests antioxidants can help clear acetaldehyde. Regular heavy drinkers also tend to have lower vitamin C levels, often because of poor diet.

### The case against it

There's no solid evidence in humans that taking vitamin C before or after drinking reduces hangover symptoms. The studies that exist are small, often test vitamin C as one ingredient in a mix, or measure lab markers rather than how people actually feel. A single night of drinking doesn't create a vitamin C deficiency in someone who eats fruit and vegetables.

### What about orange juice?

Orange juice has things going for it the morning after: fluid, some sugar if your blood sugar is low, and potassium. Any benefit you feel is more likely from those than from the vitamin C itself. It's acidic, though, so if your stomach is already irritated, water and something bland may sit better.

### How much vitamin C is safe?

The US National Institutes of Health sets the adult upper limit for vitamin C at **2,000 mg a day**. Going above that often causes diarrhea, nausea, and stomach cramps, which are not what you want when you're already hungover. People with a history of kidney stones or iron overload conditions (hemochromatosis) should be especially careful with high-dose vitamin C and check with a doctor first. Many effervescent tablets contain 1,000 mg, so two of them plus a hangover product containing vitamin C can easily push you past the limit.

**Bottom line on vitamin C:** fine to take within normal amounts, especially if your diet is short on fruit and vegetables. Don't megadose it expecting a hangover fix, because the evidence isn't there and too much will upset your stomach.

## Upper Limits: Where Stacking Products Can Go Wrong

Most water-soluble vitamins are safe because you urinate out the excess. A few have real upper limits, and hangover products often contain high doses of exactly those. These are the US adult upper limits set by the National Academies and listed by the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements:

| Vitamin | Adult upper limit | What happens above it |
|---|---|---|
| Vitamin B6 | 100 mg per day | Long-term high doses can cause nerve damage (numbness, tingling, trouble walking) |
| Niacin (B3) | 35 mg per day from supplements | Flushing, itching, stomach upset; much higher doses can stress the liver |
| Folic acid (B9) | 1,000 mcg per day from supplements | Can hide the signs of B12 deficiency while nerve damage progresses |
| Vitamin C | 2,000 mg per day | Diarrhea, nausea, cramps; kidney stone risk in susceptible people |
| Thiamine (B1) | No upper limit set | No known toxicity from oral doses |
| Vitamin B12 | No upper limit set | No known toxicity from oral doses in healthy people |

Two of these deserve a special mention for drinkers:

- **Vitamin B6.** Nerve damage from too much B6 is well documented, and some countries have recently tightened warnings about it on supplement labels. Nerve damage from heavy drinking itself looks similar (numbness and tingling in the feet and hands), so it's worth not adding a second cause. If you take a daily B-complex *and* a hangover product *and* an energy drink, add up the B6.
- **Niacin.** The niacin flush (hot, red, itchy skin) can be mistaken for an alcohol reaction. High-dose niacin is also hard on the liver, which is the organ you're already asking a lot of.

## Vitamins vs. Minerals vs. Electrolytes: Getting the Category Right

A lot of "vitamins for hangover" advice is really about minerals and electrolytes, which are a different thing.

- **Electrolytes** (sodium, potassium, chloride) control fluid balance. If you vomited or had diarrhea, replacing them along with water can genuinely help you feel better. An oral rehydration solution or a salty snack with water does this. Even here, though, research suggests the link between measured dehydration and hangover severity is weaker than most people assume.
- **Magnesium and zinc** are minerals that alcohol pushes out through the kidneys. The 2019 dietary study mentioned above linked higher zinc intake with milder hangovers. That's suggestive, not proof, and a normal diet with nuts, seeds, whole grains, and some meat or legumes covers most people.
- **Vitamins** are the B group, C, and the fat-soluble ones. As covered above, the main concern is long-term heavy drinking.

If you want a practical recovery routine, the order of priority is: fluids, food, rest, and time. Supplements come last. Our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) covers what to expect hour by hour, and if a hangover drags into the next day, see [why some hangovers last two days](/never-hungover/two-day-hangover).

## Vitamin Drips, IV Bags, and Hangover Patches

### IV vitamin drips

IV hangover drips usually contain saline plus a B-complex, vitamin C, and sometimes anti-nausea or anti-inflammatory drugs. People often feel better afterwards, but that's most likely because of the fluids and any medication included, not the vitamins. There's no good evidence that IV vitamins beat drinking water and eating breakfast for a typical hangover. IV therapy also carries small but real risks (infection, vein irritation, fluid overload in people with heart or kidney problems) and costs far more than a glass of water. If you're so dehydrated you can't keep fluids down, that's a reason to see a medical professional, not a wellness clinic.

### Vitamin patches

Hangover patches claim to deliver B vitamins and other ingredients through the skin. The skin is a strong barrier, and water-soluble vitamins like the B group don't pass through it well. There's no good evidence that these patches raise blood vitamin levels meaningfully or reduce hangovers. We look at this more closely in [do hangover patches work](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work).

## What Actually Helps a Hangover (Where Vitamins Fit)

Here's a realistic ranking of what makes a difference, from strongest to weakest evidence:

1. **Drinking less, or more slowly.** The only reliable way to prevent a hangover. Pacing drinks, alternating with water, and stopping earlier all lower peak blood alcohol.
2. **Eating before and while drinking.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood. See our guide to [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide).
3. **Choosing clearer drinks.** Vodka and gin tend to cause milder hangovers than bourbon, brandy, or red wine for the same amount of alcohol, likely because of congeners.
4. **Sleep.** Give yourself time to sleep it off when you can.
5. **Fluids and electrolytes.** Helpful, especially if you vomited, though not a complete fix.
6. **A standard dose of a pain reliever, used carefully.** Ibuprofen or similar can help a headache, but take it with food and know the stomach and kidney cautions. Avoid taking acetaminophen while drinking or in large amounts afterwards; read our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) first. More options are in our [hangover headache guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025).
7. **Supplements with some early evidence.** This includes DHM, which has animal research on alcohol metabolism and a limited amount of human data (see our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) for an honest look at what's known).
8. **Vitamins.** Useful for overall nutrition and genuinely important for heavy drinkers' long-term health, but low on the list as a hangover remedy.

If you're planning ahead for a night out, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) puts these steps together, and [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025) covers the supplement side in more detail.

## Many Hangover Products Already Contain Vitamins

Many combination hangover supplements include a B-complex alongside other ingredients. For example, [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) lists DHM, L-cysteine, milk thistle, prickly pear, a B-complex, and electrolytes. If you use a product like this, check its label before adding a separate B-complex or vitamin C so you don't double up and approach the B6 or niacin limits. And keep expectations realistic: the B vitamins in a formula like this are a supporting ingredient, not the reason to buy it, and no supplement makes heavy drinking safe.

## A Sensible Vitamin Approach for Different Drinkers

### If you drink occasionally (a few times a month or less)

- You don't need a special vitamin routine for drinking.
- A daily multivitamin or B-complex is optional and won't hurt if you stay under the upper limits.
- Spend your effort on eating before drinking, pacing, water, and sleep.

### If you drink regularly but moderately

- A daily B-complex or multivitamin is reasonable insurance, particularly if your diet is uneven.
- Pay attention to food quality: leafy greens and legumes for folate, whole grains and pork for thiamine, fruit and vegetables for vitamin C, nuts and seeds for magnesium.
- Watch the totals if you also take hangover products or energy drinks.

### If you drink heavily most days

- This is the group for whom vitamins, especially thiamine, really matter, and also the group for whom self-treatment is least appropriate.
- Talk to a doctor. They can check for deficiencies, recommend the right thiamine dose, and help with cutting down safely. Stopping suddenly after long, heavy drinking can cause dangerous withdrawal and should be done with medical support.
- Know the warning signs of thiamine deficiency (confusion, unsteadiness, unusual eye movements, numb or tingling feet) and treat them as urgent.

### Pregnancy, medication, and medical conditions

If you're pregnant or trying to conceive, the safest amount of alcohol is none, and your folate needs should be guided by your doctor or midwife. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before starting any supplement, including vitamins. Some interactions are real; for example, high-dose folic acid and B6 can affect some anti-seizure medicines, and vitamin C can affect the absorption of some drugs. People with kidney disease should not take high-dose vitamin C without medical advice.

## The Bottom Line

Alcohol does increase vitamin and mineral losses, and over time heavy drinking causes genuine, sometimes dangerous deficiencies, with thiamine the most serious. But a hangover after an occasional night out is not a vitamin deficiency, and there's no strong evidence that B-complex, thiamine, or vitamin C pills prevent or cure one. A daily multivitamin is a fine, inexpensive habit if your diet needs it. If you drink heavily on a regular basis, the most protective thing you can do is talk to a doctor about thiamine and about your drinking.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What vitamins are good for a hangover?**

No vitamin has strong evidence as a hangover cure. B vitamins and vitamin C are the most commonly used, and taking them within normal amounts is low-risk, but trials haven't shown that they reliably reduce symptoms. Fluids, food, sleep, and drinking less make a much bigger difference. Vitamins matter more for long-term health in people who drink heavily, especially thiamine (B1).

**Does vitamin C help a hangover?**

There's no solid human evidence that vitamin C prevents or treats hangovers. It's an antioxidant and has shown some protective effects in animal studies, but that hasn't translated into proven relief in people. Normal amounts are fine. Stay under the 2,000 mg daily upper limit, since higher doses commonly cause diarrhea and stomach cramps, and check with a doctor first if you've had kidney stones.

**Should I take a B-complex before or after drinking?**

Timing makes little practical difference, because there's no good evidence that a B-complex changes how you'll feel the next morning. If you want to take one, taking it with a meal is easiest on the stomach and helps absorption. Check the label of any hangover product you also use so you don't exceed 100 mg of B6 or 35 mg of supplemental niacin a day.

**Does alcohol deplete thiamine (vitamin B1)?**

Yes, especially with regular heavy drinking. Alcohol reduces how much thiamine your gut absorbs, how much your liver stores, and how well your body activates it, and heavy drinkers often eat less. Over time this can lead to Wernicke's encephalopathy, a medical emergency marked by confusion, unsteady walking, and abnormal eye movements. One night of drinking won't make a healthy, well-fed person deficient.

**Should heavy drinkers take thiamine?**

Many doctors recommend thiamine for people who drink heavily, and clinical guidelines advise it for people being treated for alcohol dependence. Oral thiamine is inexpensive and has no established upper limit. But anyone drinking heavily should talk to a doctor rather than rely on a supplement alone, both to get the right dose and because severe deficiency often needs injected thiamine.

**Do IV vitamin drips cure hangovers?**

People often feel better after an IV drip, but that's most likely from the fluids and any anti-nausea medicine included, not the vitamins. There's no good evidence that IV vitamins work better than drinking water, eating, and resting for a typical hangover, and IV therapy carries small risks and a high cost. If you can't keep fluids down, see a medical professional.

**Does a multivitamin help with drinking?**

A multivitamin can help cover gaps in your diet, which is useful if you drink regularly and don't eat well. It won't prevent a hangover, protect your liver from heavy drinking, or make drinking safer. It's a reasonable everyday habit, not a drinking strategy.

**Can you take too many vitamins for a hangover?**

Yes. Vitamin B6 above 100 mg a day over time can cause nerve damage, supplemental niacin above 35 mg a day causes flushing and stomach upset, and vitamin C above 2,000 mg a day causes digestive problems. Hangover products, energy drinks, and daily vitamins often overlap, so add up the totals from everything you take.
